{{Short description|American logician}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=July 2025}}
'''Steven Kuhn''' is an American [[philosophy]] professor at [[Georgetown University]] whose research focuses on [[logic]], [[ethics]] and the [[philosophy of language]].<ref>{{Cite web |url= https://gufaculty360.georgetown.edu/s/faculty-profile?netid=kuhns/|title=Faculty|last=|first=|date=|website=[[Georgetown University]]|language=en|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=2018-09-02}}</ref>

==Career==
Kuhn earned his undergraduate degree in [[mathematics]] from [[Johns Hopkins University]] and his [[Ph.D.]] from [[Stanford University]]. Prior to his position at Georgetown, he taught at the [[University of Michigan]], [[UCLA]] and the [[University of Pennsylvania]].

Kuhn is the author of the two-volume ''Many-sorted Modal Logics'' (1977) and contributed the article on the [[prisoner's dilemma]] to the ''[[Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |url= https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/spr2017/entries/prisoner-dilemma/|title=Prisoner's Dilemma|last=Kuhn|first=Steven|date=2014-08-29|website=[[Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy]]|archive-url=|archive-date= |access-date=2018-09-02}}</ref>

=== Moral philosophy and game theory ===
Kuhn has written extensively on the [[prisoner's dilemma]]. In his article 'Pure and Utilitarian Prisoner's dilemmas',<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/economics-and-philosophy/article/abs/pure-and-utilitarian-prisoners-dilemmas/E62EE5804FCBB107D341D984E0F0605D | doi=10.1017/S0266267100003424 | title=Pure and Utilitarian Prisoner's Dilemmas | date=1995 | last1=Kuhn | first1=Steven T. | last2=Moresi | first2=Serge | journal=Economics and Philosophy | volume=11 | issue=2 | pages=333–343 | url-access=subscription }}</ref> he distinguishes between a 'pure' prisoner's dilemma and an impure prisoner's dilemma. A "pure dilemma" is defined when no mixed strategies improve outcomes over mutual cooperation; it's an "impure dilemma" when such strategies exist. This distinction is interesting since in the case of an "impure dilemma", individuals who do not consistently follow moral rules can gain an advantage over individuals who do. Therefore, the possibility that moral behaviour requires randomization of one's actions arises.

In his subsequent paper "The Impure Game: Feasible Payoffs and Possible Generalizations", Kuhn attempts to extend the concept of impurity to other games, such as the [[Chicken (game)|Chicken Game]] and the [[Battle of the sexes (game theory)|Battle of the Sexes]].<ref>Steven Kuhn, [https://steven-t-kuhn.weebly.com/uploads/1/2/6/7/126730899/theimpuregame.pdf "The Impure Game: Feasible Payoffs and Possible Generalizations].</ref>

Kuhn has pointed out two obstacles towards the synthesis between [[game theory]] and [[ethics]] first suggested by [[R. B. Braithwaite]]. Firstly, he argues that there is a lack of careful consideration in choosing the most suitable game theoretic framework and in interpreting the technical tools used in these discussions. Second, he cites some challenging examples from game theory. <ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kuhn |first=Steven T. |date=July 2004 |title=Reflections on Ethics and Game Theory |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1023/B:SYNT.0000035846.91195.cb |journal=Synthese |language=en |volume=141 |issue=1 |pages=1–44 |doi=10.1023/B:SYNT.0000035846.91195.cb |issn=0039-7857|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Kuhn then points out that even in a pure dilemma, if utilities are transferable (i.e., one can compensate the other), universal cooperation might not be the optimal collective strategy. The scenario with possible utility transfers that benefit both players is termed a "nonutilitarian dilemma," and "utilitarian dilemma" otherwise. These distinctions in the prisoner's dilemma have practical implications, such as in the formulation of moral rules or the structuring of legal contracts, where the type of dilemma can influence recommended or optimal behaviors.

In "The Pragmatics of Tense", Kuhn argues applies a framework inspired by Montague's to analyze the English tense system, suggesting that shared knowledge impacts the use of tenses, hence the use of the word [[pragmatics]]. This principle, Kuhn argues, could also apply to other linguistic elements such as pronouns and ambiguity.<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00485679 | doi=10.1007/BF00485679 | title=The pragmatics of tense | date=1979 | last1=Kuhn | first1=Steven | journal=Synthese | volume=40 | issue=2 | pages=231–263 | url-access=subscription }}</ref>

He has 1084 citations and an [[h-index]] of 13 on [[Google Scholar]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=YLazs68AAAAJ&hl=en | title=Steve Kuhn }}</ref>
